title: The turner at the lathe
hookLine: as a skilled turner knows a long pull and a short pull (MN 10)

lines: A BARBER, A BAKER, A CARPENTER.
cards: Watch someone who's really good at a craft. A barber with the clippers. A baker shaping loaves.
A carpenter planing a board. They aren't tense, and they aren't daydreaming either. Their hands know exactly what they're doing, stroke by stroke, and it looks almost easy.
Right in the middle of the breathing instructions, the Satipatthana Sutta stops to give a picture like that, from a workshop most people have never seen.

teach.h: A TURNER SHAPES WOOD ON A LATHE.
teach.b: A turner is a woodworker who shapes wood on a lathe, spinning it while a blade carves it round: bowls, legs for a stool, beads. The sutta says: like a skilled turner, or a turner's apprentice.
Making a long turn, he knows, I make a long turn. Making a short turn, he knows, I make a short turn.
In the same way, the one who meditates, breathing in long, knows I breathe in long; breathing in short, knows I breathe in short. The sutta doesn't describe the machine.
It only says the turner knows each pull, long or short, as it happens, all day long. So the picture has a rhythm, like the breath. The image adds three things.
First, skill. The turner isn't straining to notice each pull; in skilled hands, the knowing is built in. Mindfulness of breathing is meant to become like that: a skill, not a strain.
Second, the turner knows without stopping to comment.
No 'what a lovely long pull, I'm so good at this.' Just knowing, and working. Third, the knowing serves the work.
A turner who lost track of the pull would ruin the bowl. The breath works the same way. Knowing it isn't an extra task on top of breathing.

how: Teachers of mindfulness of breathing often use the sutta's image of the skilled turner to explain that the aim is plain, steady knowing of each breath, like a craftsperson's attention, rather than effortful control.

o: forcing the breath into a perfect rhythm
a talent you're born with or simply don't have
knowing that's built in, without strain or comment

games.q: match each piece of the turner simile.
p: a long breath, known as long

s: the turner simile describes controlling the breath
the turner simply knows each long or short pull; the breath is known, not forced.
the simile appears in the middle of the breathing instructions
right after long and short breaths, in MN 10.
the skilled turner comments on every pull
the point is knowing without commentary, the way skilled hands work.

games.q: you're meditating and start thinking, 'that was a great long breath, I'm getting good at this.' what would the turner do?
o: stop meditating to think about progress.
just know the next pull, long or short, and keep working.
games.why: the turner knows each pull without comment. the knowing serves the work; the commentary interrupts it.

practice: Let each breath be a pull at the turner's lathe, a pull in, a pull out, some long, some short. Just know which is which, the way the turner's hands know, without comment and without changing the breath.
If a commentary starts up, let it go, and come back to the next pull.

wordCard.voice: Skill. Mindfulness of breathing is meant to become this, not a strain: the skilled woodworker knows each long pull and each short pull, and the meditator knows each breath the same way.

carryVoice: Your line: the turner knows. Skilled hands know without narrating. Two hundred forty-nine days in.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the turner simile
